A Purpose and Scope of the Triage Guide
This guide sets how incoming service
tickets are classified, prioritised and passed
between shifts so that nothing is dropped at
handover. It applies to every queue in the
service desk and to all staff who triage, own
or receive tickets. The aim is consistent
decisions: the same ticket should reach the
same severity and owner regardless of who
is on duty. Where local practice differs, the
stricter rule applies until the guide is
formally revised.
A.1 Intake Channels and
Ticket Registration
Tickets arrive by portal form, email, phone
and walk-in. Each channel is registered in
the same system within the same working
day, and the registrar records the
requester, the affected service, the
observed symptom and any deadline
already promised. Email and phone reports
must be transcribed into the ticket body
rather than left in a mailbox. Duplicate
reports of one incident are linked to a
parent ticket so counts stay honest.

A.1.1 Initial Classification and
Severity Rules
Table 1: Comparison of intake channels and their
registration duties
Classification starts with the affected
service and the reported impact, not with
the loudest requester. Triage assigns a
category, a severity and an initial owner,
then checks whether an open incident
already covers the symptom. Severity
reflects breadth and business effect: a
single user blocked differs from a whole site
unable to work. When evidence is thin,
triage records what is unknown and sets a
short review point instead of guessing.
A.1.1.1 Severity Assignment and
Escalation Triggers
Severity levels run from routine to critical,
and each level carries a response
expectation and an escalation trigger.
Triggers include multiple reports of one
symptom, a service with no workaround, or
a requester deadline that cannot be met
within the normal queue. Escalation moves
the ticket to a named senior owner and
notifies the duty lead. Downgrades require
a written reason, because quiet

reclassification hides demand and distorts
later reporting.
A.1.1.1.1 Ownership, Queue
Assignment and Response Clock
Every ticket has one accountable owner at
any moment, even when several teams
contribute. Assignment follows the service
catalogue: the queue that owns the failing
component takes the ticket, and assisting
teams are recorded as contributors. The
response clock starts at registration and
pauses only for documented requester
input. Owners must acknowledge within the
published expectation and record the first
diagnostic step taken, so the next person
inherits evidence rather than a blank page.

and escalation triggers
A.1.1.1.1.1 First Response and
Diagnostic Checklist
The first response confirms the symptom,
checks the service status page, and runs
the standard diagnostic checklist for the
category. The owner records what was
tested, what was observed, and what was
ruled out. If the checklist resolves the issue,
the ticket closes with the resolution note; if
not, the owner states the next hypothesis
and the evidence needed. Speculation is
welcome only when labelled as such.
A.1.1.1.1.2 Requester
Communication and Expectation
Setting
Requesters receive a plain-language
acknowledgement that names the owner,
restates the symptom as understood, and
gives the next update point. Updates are
sent at each state change and before any
promised deadline passes, even when the
news is that work continues. Staff avoid
promising fix times they do not control;
they promise update times instead.
Sensitive tickets use approved wording and
never expose internal hostnames or
colleague names.
A.1.1.1.2 Reassignment and Cross
Team Handoff
Reassignment is a transfer of
accountability, not a forward of the ticket.
The outgoing owner writes a handoff note
covering symptom, evidence gathered,
hypotheses tested, current workaround and
the exact next action. The incoming owner
accepts explicitly before the clock resumes.
If the receiving queue disputes ownership,
the duty lead decides within the same shift
and records the decision, so the ticket
never bounces silently between teams.

A.1.1.2 Documentation Standards
for Triage Notes
Notes must let a stranger continue the work
without asking questions. Each entry states
the time, the actor, the action taken and
the result observed. Free-text opinions are
separated from recorded evidence, and
links to logs or screenshots are preferred
over pasted excerpts. Notes avoid
abbreviations that only one team
understands. At closure the resolution note
explains the cause as far as it is known and
flags anything still unproven.
A.1.2 Quality Review of
Classification Decisions
A sample of closed tickets is reviewed each
period against the severity rules and
documentation standards. Reviewers check
whether severity matched impact, whether
ownership was clear at every stage, and
whether handoff notes were sufficient.
Findings feed a short coaching note to the
relevant team rather than a blame list.
Recurring misclassification points to a rule
that needs clarifying, and the guide is
amended accordingly.
A.2 Triage Metrics and
Reporting Discipline
Reporting covers volume by category,
response against expectation,
reassignment counts and reopened tickets.
Metrics describe the queue, not individual
worth, and are read alongside the review
findings. A rising reassignment rate usually
signals unclear ownership boundaries
rather than poor staff. Reports are shared
with team leads monthly, and any metric
used in planning must be defined in the
same document so nobody argues about
definitions after the fact.
B Shift Handover
Procedure
Handover happens at fixed times and
follows a fixed shape: open critical tickets
first, then tickets awaiting requester input,
then work in progress. The outgoing shift
reads each note aloud and the incoming
shift confirms understanding. Anything
ambiguous is resolved before the outgoing
shift leaves. The handover record lists the
tickets discussed, the agreed next actions
and who holds each one, and is stored with
the shift log.
B.1 Handover Note Contents
and Format
Each handover entry names the ticket, its
severity, its owner, the last confirmed
observation and the next action with a time.
It states what the requester was last told,
so the next shift does not contradict a
promise. Open questions and suspected

causes are listed separately from confirmed
facts. Entries are short enough to read
under pressure but complete enough that
no one needs to reopen the whole ticket
history.
Supporting records are presented in Figure
B.1.1 Critical Ticket Continuity
Across Shifts
Critical tickets never wait for a convenient
handover. The outgoing owner briefs the
incoming owner directly, confirms access to
the working channels, and stays reachable
for a short overlap. The incoming owner
restates the current hypothesis and the
next diagnostic step before taking over. If
no incoming owner is available, the duty
lead is named as interim owner and that
decision is recorded with a time.
B.1.1.1 Escalation Paths During
Handover
During handover the escalation path must
be known without consulting a directory.
The handover record names the duty lead,
the on-call engineer for each affected
service and the communications contact for
requester updates. If an escalation trigger
fires mid-handover, the incoming shift owns
it from the moment of acceptance, and the
outgoing shift supports until the duty lead
confirms the transfer is complete.
B.1.1.1.1 Open Work Tracking and
Carryover Rules
Work that cannot finish within a shift is
carried over deliberately, not by default.
Carryover requires a live owner, a stated
next action and a reason the work paused.
Tickets awaiting requester input are parked
with a follow-up date rather than carried as
active work. The handover record
distinguishes active carryover from parked
items, so the incoming shift knows what
genuinely needs attention first.
B.1.1.1.1.1 Handover Checklist and
Sign-Off
The checklist is short and mandatory: every
critical ticket briefed, every carryover item
owned, every promise to a requester
visible, and every escalation contact
confirmed. Both shifts sign the handover
record, and the signature means the
incoming shift accepts the listed items, not
that the outgoing shift is absolved of errors
found later. Unsigned handovers are
treated as incomplete and raised with the
duty lead.

Recovery Steps

shift accepts a handover
When a handover is missed, the incoming
shift reconstructs state from the ticket
notes and the shift log before touching any
SYNTHETIC DOCUMENT | RESEARCH PROTOTYPE
ticket. The duty lead is informed
immediately, and any requester promise
that has already lapsed is addressed first.
The recovery record notes the gap, what
was reconstructed and what remains
uncertain. A repeated missed handover
triggers a review of shift scheduling rather
than a reminder to try harder.
B.1.1.1.2 Training New Staff on
Handover Practice
New staff shadow two handovers before
leading one, and their first led handover is
observed by a senior colleague. Training
covers note writing, the checklist,
escalation contacts and the difference
between active carryover and parked work.
Trainees practise reconstructing a ticket
from notes alone, which exposes gaps
quickly. Competence is confirmed by the
observer, not by attendance at a briefing
session.
B.1.1.2 Audit Trail and Record
Retention
Handover records, triage notes and closure
summaries form the audit trail and are
retained under the records schedule.
Records must show who decided what and
when, without exposing unnecessary
personal data. Corrections are appended,
never overwritten, and the reason for each
correction is stated. Audit requests are
answered from these records, so
completeness at the time of writing matters
more than tidiness later.

Table 5: Records retained for audit and the reason
each is kept
B.1.2 Continuous Improvement of
Triage Practice
Improvements come from review findings,
recurring ticket patterns and staff
suggestions gathered at handover. Each
proposed change names the problem it
solves and the evidence behind it, and is
trialled for a defined period before
adoption. The guide is versioned, and every
change is announced with the date it takes
effect. Practices that no longer earn their
effort are retired openly rather than left to
linger.
B.2 Governance, Roles and
Review Cycle
The service desk manager owns this guide,
team leads maintain the category and
severity rules, and the duty lead arbitrates
ownership disputes. The guide is reviewed
on a fixed cycle and after any critical
incident that exposed a gap. Proposed
amendments are circulated to all queues
for comment before approval. Approved
changes are communicated, trained where
needed, and recorded in the version history
with the effective date.
